title: Radial Profiling of Dense Molecular Gas and Continuum Emission in the Nucleus of NGC 4429: A Beam-Limited Test for a Circumnuclear HCN(1-0) Deficit Yields a Compact Continuum Core but Inconclusive Gas Constraints
abstract: Some early-type galaxies with circumnuclear molecular disks show evidence for a central depression in dense-gas tracers relative to lower-density CO, potentially linked to AGN feedback or dynamical clearing, but testing this at the true cavity scale requires angular resolution finer than is often available. We used two ALMA science-ready products for NGC 4429 (Virgo Cluster, adopted distance 16.5 Mpc) — a Band 3 continuum image (beam 1.63 x 1.55 arcsec) and an HCN(1-0) cube (beam 1.88 x 1.81 arcsec, 49.5 km/s channels, systemic velocity 1104 km/s) — to measure azimuthally averaged radial profiles in circular apertures of 1, 2, and 3 beam radii (147, 295, and 442 pc) centered on the known nucleus, after standard noise characterization, moment-map construction, and PV-diagram analysis. The Band 3 continuum was detected at all three radii (0.927 +/- 0.084, 1.069 +/- 0.168, and 0.852 +/- 0.254 mJy; S/N of 11.0, 6.4, and 3.4 respectively), indicating a compact nuclear source rather than a continuum-faint nucleus. In contrast, HCN(1-0) was not detected at any radius: the 1-, 2-, and 3-beam apertures and the 1-3 beam annulus yielded only 3-sigma upper limits (dense-gas mass limits of 8.7e6, 1.7e7, and 2.6e7 Msun using alpha_HCN = 10 Msun / (K km/s pc^2)), with the central-to-annulus log-luminosity ratio of -0.444 reflecting two non-detections rather than a resolved deficit. We therefore cannot distinguish a genuine central depression in dense gas from an overall HCN(1-0)-faint nucleus given the sensitivity and representative-bandwidth coverage of this cube; a moment-1 velocity range of 804-1399 km/s across marginally significant pixels is consistent with, but does not confirm, the known circumnuclear disk rotation. These results demonstrate that a compact dust- or AGN-associated continuum core coexists with an HCN(1-0) reservoir too faint (or too spatially/spectrally diluted) to test the proposed dense-gas cavity at beam-limited resolution, underscoring the need for deeper and/or higher-resolution HCN observations to resolve the true nuclear gas structure.
introduction:
Circumnuclear molecular disks are common features of nearby early-type galaxies, tracing the reservoir of gas that fuels nuclear star formation, feeds a central black hole, or simply persists as a dynamically settled structure left over from an accretion event. These disks are most often mapped in CO, a comparatively low-critical-density tracer that lights up wherever molecular gas of essentially any density resides. Denser gas tracers such as HCN(1-0), with a critical density roughly two to three orders of magnitude higher than CO, instead pick out the gas most directly implicated in star formation and in fueling accretion onto a central engine. In several early-type galaxies with well-studied circumnuclear disks, comparisons between CO and dense-gas tracers have revealed a suggestive pattern: a central depression or "hole" in the dense-gas distribution that is not mirrored in the total molecular gas traced by CO. Proposed explanations include AGN feedback evacuating or heating the densest gas near the nucleus, tidal or dynamical clearing associated with a central mass concentration, or a genuine change in the physical conditions of the gas as it approaches the potential minimum. Distinguishing between these scenarios, or even confirming that such a deficit is real rather than an artifact of limited sensitivity or resolution, requires resolving the gas distribution on the physical scale of the putative cavity itself, typically of order tens of parsecs.

This requirement is difficult to satisfy in practice. Dense-gas cavities of this kind are usually reported on scales that are only marginally larger than, or comparable to, the synthesized beam of the interferometric observations available to test them. When the beam size approaches or exceeds the cavity scale, any genuine central depression is diluted by flux from surrounding disk material falling within the same resolution element, biasing the observed profile toward flatness regardless of the true underlying distribution. Compounding this, HCN(1-0) is intrinsically faint relative to CO in most galaxies, so achieving the sensitivity needed to detect or rule out a depression, rather than simply failing to detect the line at all, often demands deep integrations that are not always available in archival or pipeline-processed data products. A non-detection of dense gas near the nucleus is therefore ambiguous on its face: it could indicate an evacuated cavity, a source that is simply faint in HCN throughout, or a signal that has been suppressed by insufficient velocity coverage in a given observation. Any attempt to test for a central dense-gas deficit using modest-resolution, modest-depth data must therefore be explicit about which of these possibilities its data can and cannot distinguish, rather than treating a non-detection as evidence of a hole by default.

NGC 4429 is a lenticular galaxy in the Virgo Cluster hosting a well-established circumnuclear molecular disk, making it a natural test case for this question. Archival ALMA observations provide two science-ready products for this galaxy: a Band 3 continuum image and an HCN(1-0) cube, both with beam sizes of order 1.5-2 arcsec, corresponding to roughly 150-300 pc at the adopted distance of 16.5 Mpc. This resolution is coarser than the sub-100-pc scale on which a dense-gas cavity would be expected to reside, so any test conducted with these products is necessarily a beam-limited one: it can assess whether the nuclear region is depressed, flat, or enhanced in dense gas relative to its surroundings at the scale the data actually resolve, but it cannot directly confirm or rule out a genuinely sub-beam cavity. The HCN cube is additionally a "representative bandwidth" product with reduced velocity coverage relative to a full science observation, which limits the range of line widths and velocity offsets that can be captured and must be considered when interpreting any non-detection.

This study uses these two data products to construct azimuthally averaged radial profiles of HCN(1-0) and Band 3 continuum emission around the known nuclear position of NGC 4429, using circular apertures scaled to the beam size at radii of one, two, and three beam widths. Standard noise characterization, moment-map construction, and position-velocity analysis are used to assess the significance of any emission in each aperture, with detections reported where the signal-to-noise ratio permits and three-sigma upper limits reported otherwise, in both flux and derived dense-gas mass. The central aperture is compared against the surrounding annulus to quantify whether the profile is consistent with a depression, a flat distribution, or a beam-diluted concentration, and the Band 3 continuum profile is measured in parallel to test independently whether the nucleus hosts a compact source, which would itself constrain the plausibility of an actively fed or heated center. Kinematic information from the moment maps and position-velocity diagram is used as a secondary, qualitative check on whether any detected emission is consistent with ordered rotation in the known disk.

Success in this study is not defined by detecting a cavity, but by determining, as precisely as the data allow, which of the possible outcomes the observations support: a resolved central deficit in dense gas relative to the surrounding disk, a flat or centrally concentrated profile that argues against such a deficit at the scales probed, or an inconclusive result in which the sensitivity and bandwidth of the available cube are insufficient to distinguish between these possibilities. Each of these outcomes is reported together with the beam-scale and bandwidth caveats needed to interpret it correctly, and the continuum measurement is used throughout as an independent line of evidence on the nature of the nuclear region, so that the dense-gas constraint and the compact-source question are evaluated jointly rather than in isolation.
methods:
### Data products and analysis environment

The analysis was carried out on the two delivered, primary-beam-corrected ALMA data products for NGC 4429: the Band 3 continuum image and the HCN(1–0) spectral cube. Both products were loaded into a Python analysis environment using `spectral-cube`, `astropy`, `radio_beam`, and `photutils.aperture`. The WCS headers, pixel scale, synthesized beam parameters, and rest frequency (88.6316 GHz for HCN(1–0)) recorded in the FITS headers were checked against the values quoted in the data description before proceeding. The cube's spectral axis was converted from frequency to velocity, referenced to the systemic velocity of NGC 4429 (heliocentric, taken from NED), for use in all subsequent moment-map, PV-diagram, and channel-selection steps.

### Noise characterization

The per-channel RMS noise of the HCN(1–0) cube was measured from line-free channels away from the systemic velocity, and a continuum RMS was measured from a source-free region of the Band 3 image. These RMS measurements were carried forward as the basis for every signal-to-noise calculation, detection threshold, and upper limit computed in later steps.

### Masking and moment maps

A signal mask was constructed for the HCN(1–0) cube using `spectral_cube.masking` utilities, following a dilated-mask approach with a 3–4σ core threshold and a 2σ dilation threshold. This mask was applied to produce moment 0 (integrated intensity), moment 1 (intensity-weighted velocity), and moment 2 (velocity dispersion) maps of the HCN(1–0) emission. Because masked emission was found to be marginal, the unmasked cube was retained and used directly for the aperture-based flux and limit measurements described below, rather than relying solely on the moment 0 map. A position–velocity diagram was also constructed by cutting a slice through the cube along the major axis of the previously known circumnuclear molecular disk, using the position angle given in the archive/proposal description of the disk geometry.

### Nuclear coordinate frame and beam-scaled apertures

The nucleus was fixed at RA = 12:27:26.503, Dec = +11:06:27.58 using `astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord`, and this position was checked against the continuum peak and against the kinematic center implied by the moment 1 map and PV diagram. Using the geometric-mean FWHM of the synthesized beam as the effective beam size for each data product (measured independently for the HCN cube and the continuum image, since the two beams differ slightly), concentric circular apertures were defined at radii of 1, 2, and 3 beam-widths centered on the nucleus. Angular radii were converted to physical scale adopting a distance of 16.5 Mpc (Virgo Cluster mean, NGVS SBF catalog), so that each aperture radius is reported in both arcseconds and parsecs.

### Radial intensity profile, detection/limit rule, and mass conversion

For each aperture, `photutils.aperture` circular-aperture photometry was applied to the HCN(1–0) cube. Because the masked moment 0 map contained marginal signal, flux was extracted from the unmasked cube by integrating over a fixed velocity window centered on the systemic velocity and matched to the searched channel range, with the per-channel RMS and number of summed channels propagated to a formal uncertainty and signal-to-noise ratio for each aperture. Apertures reaching signal-to-noise ≥ 3 were to be reported as detections with flux and formal uncertainty; apertures below this threshold were reported instead as 3σ upper limits computed over the same velocity window and aperture area, with the assumed velocity width stated explicitly. The same aperture photometry procedure was applied to the Band 3 continuum image at the corresponding beam-scaled radii, using the continuum RMS from Step 1 to obtain a flux density and uncertainty (or 3σ upper limit) at each radius.

Each HCN(1–0) flux value or upper limit was converted to a line luminosity, L′_HCN, in units of K km/s pc², using the standard Solomon & Vanden Bout-style luminosity formula with the adopted source distance and observed rest frequency. Each luminosity or luminosity limit was then converted to a dense-gas mass or mass limit using a fixed α_HCN conversion factor of 10.0 M_sun / (K km/s pc²) (Gao & Solomon 2004), applied uniformly as a documented unit-conversion constant rather than a target-specific fit. The resulting radial flux/limit table and the derived luminosity/mass table were tabulated together, and the radial profile (flux or limit versus radius in beams, arcseconds, and parsecs) was plotted with detections and limits marked distinctly.

### Central-depression metric

The innermost (1-beam-radius) aperture measurement or limit was compared against an annulus spanning 1–3 beam radii to assess whether the HCN(1–0) radial profile is flat, centrally peaked, or centrally depressed within the measurement or limit uncertainties. This comparison was framed explicitly as a beam-scale test, given that the beam size is comparable to or larger than the previously reported CO(2–1) cavity scale: the result was categorized as consistent with a central deficit, consistent with a beam-diluted but present central concentration, or inconclusive given the limit depth, rather than as a firm detection or non-detection of any sub-beam cavity. The metric used was the base-10 logarithmic ratio of the central-aperture luminosity (or limit) to the 1–3 beam annulus luminosity (or limit), with uncertainties or limits propagated through the ratio.

### Kinematic cross-check

The moment 1 map and PV diagram produced in the masking/moment-map step were used to assess, qualitatively, whether HCN(1–0) emission in and around the central apertures follows the ordered rotation pattern expected from the known circumnuclear molecular disk — i.e., a smooth velocity gradient along the previously established disk position angle — or instead shows a velocity signature offset from that pattern (elevated dispersion, an asymmetric or double-peaked profile, or a feature offset from systemic velocity) suggestive of non-circular motion. This step was carried out as a descriptive diagnostic layered on the existing moment and PV products, with no dynamical modeling or mass fitting performed.

### Continuum cross-check

The beam-scaled circular-aperture photometry procedure was repeated on the Band 3 continuum image at the same nucleus coordinates and the same 1-, 2-, and 3-beam-radius apertures (scaled to the continuum beam), with the continuum RMS from Step 1 propagated to a flux density measurement with uncertainty or a 3σ upper limit at each radius. This radial continuum profile was compared to the surrounding annuli to test whether the nucleus is consistent with a compact, spatially unresolved or marginally resolved continuum source versus emission consistent with the surrounding diffuse level, and is reported alongside the HCN(1–0) radial profile as an independent constraint on the nature of the nucleus. No spectral index or SED modeling was attempted, consistent with the single-band nature of the continuum image.

### Synthesis

All quantitative results were tied directly to RMS and beam values measured from the two named FITS products themselves, with the sole external inputs being the adopted distance (16.5 Mpc, Virgo Cluster mean, NGVS SBF catalog) and the α_HCN conversion factor (10.0 M_sun / (K km/s pc²), Gao & Solomon 2004). Every case in which an aperture measurement fell below the 3σ detection threshold was logged as a non-detection subject to the limited velocity coverage of the representative-bandwidth HCN cube, so that "no dense gas present" could be distinguished from "dense gas present but undetected given this cube's bandwidth and sensitivity."
results:
### Band 3 Continuum

A nuclear continuum source was detected in NGC 4429 at Band 3 (synthesized beam 1.63 x 1.55 arcsec, PA 80.4 deg; RMS 0.0440 mJy/beam). Aperture photometry centered on the nucleus (Figure 1) yielded a detection at all three tested aperture radii, with flux density decreasing in significance as aperture size increased:

- r = 1 beam (1.84 arcsec = 147 pc): 0.927 +/- 0.084 mJy (S/N = 11.0)
- r = 2 beam (3.68 arcsec = 295 pc): 1.069 +/- 0.168 mJy (S/N = 6.4)
- r = 3 beam (5.52 arcsec = 442 pc): 0.852 +/- 0.254 mJy (S/N = 3.4)

### HCN(1-0)

The HCN(1-0) cube (rest frequency 88.6316 GHz; beam 1.88 x 1.81 arcsec, PA 79.8 deg; per-channel RMS 0.848 mJy/beam; 13 channels of 49.5 km/s width searched over +/-300 km/s about the adopted systemic velocity of 1104 km/s) did not yield a significant line detection in any aperture (Figure 2). Integrated flux measurements, expressed as 3-sigma upper limits, were:

- r = 1 beam (147 pc): 0.765 +/- 0.255 Jy km/s (S/N = 1.47); L'_HCN = 8.684e+05 K km/s pc^2; dense-gas mass = 8.684e+06 Msun (adopting alpha_HCN = 10.0 Msun / (K km/s pc^2))
- r = 2 beam (295 pc): 1.515 +/- 0.505 Jy km/s (S/N = 2.23); L'_HCN = 1.720e+06 K km/s pc^2; dense-gas mass = 1.720e+07 Msun
- r = 3 beam (442 pc): 2.261 +/- 0.754 Jy km/s (S/N = 1.86); L'_HCN = 2.566e+06 K km/s pc^2; dense-gas mass = 2.566e+07 Msun

The 1-3 beam annulus (i.e., the region between the r = 1 and r = 3 beam apertures) gave an integrated flux 3-sigma upper limit of 2.128 Jy km/s.

### Central Depression Metric

The log10 ratio of the central (r = 1 beam) aperture to the 1-3 beam annulus flux was -0.444. Both the central aperture and the annulus are non-detections at the sensitivity achieved, so this ratio cannot distinguish a genuine central deficit in HCN(1-0) emission from an overall HCN(1-0)-faint nucleus; the result is inconclusive given the depth of the limits.

### Kinematics

Across the searched velocity range, 383 spatial pixels exceeded the 3-sigma per-channel threshold, with moment-1 velocities spanning 804 to 1399 km/s about the systemic velocity of 1104 km/s (Figure 3). Given that the integrated HCN(1-0) flux in all three apertures constitutes a non-detection (upper limits only, S/N < 3 in every case), these per-pixel exceedances do not constitute a significant, spatially coherent line detection, and the position-velocity structure in Figure 3 cannot be used to characterize rotation or any other organized kinematic pattern in HCN(1-0) at the current sensitivity.
conclusions:
This pilot study set out to test whether NGC 4429's circumnuclear molecular disk shows a central depression in dense gas relative to CO, using two archival, science-ready ALMA products at beam-limited resolution. The Band 3 continuum results are unambiguous: a compact source is detected at the nucleus at all three tested radii, with declining significance at larger aperture (S/N of 11.0, 6.4, and 3.4 at 1, 2, and 3 beam radii), consistent with a genuine compact dust- or AGN-associated nuclear source rather than a continuum-faint or diffuse center. This establishes that the nucleus of NGC 4429 is not devoid of compact emission at these scales, independent of the dense-gas question.

The HCN(1-0) results, by contrast, do not establish a detection or a non-detection of the proposed dense-gas cavity. All three apertures and the 1-3 beam annulus returned only 3-sigma upper limits, and the resulting central-to-annulus log-luminosity ratio of -0.444 compares two non-detections rather than two measured fluxes. This number cannot be read as evidence of a central deficit, since an equally faint but spatially uniform HCN(1-0) distribution would produce a similar or even more negative ratio purely from noise. The moment-1 map's apparent velocity range of 804-1399 km/s is suggestive of the known disk rotation but rests on marginally significant pixels rather than a coherent line detection, so it cannot be used to confirm kinematic structure. Taken together, the data support only the weakest of the three possible outcomes defined at the outset: an inconclusive result, in which the nuclear region's true HCN(1-0) distribution — depressed, flat, or centrally concentrated — remains unresolved by this cube.

Two limitations of the available data drive this ambiguity and should be weighed explicitly rather than treated as generic caveats. First, the beam sizes used here (1.63 x 1.55 arcsec for the continuum, 1.88 x 1.81 arcsec for HCN, corresponding to roughly 147-295 pc even at the smallest aperture) are coarse relative to the ~10-100 pc scale on which dense-gas cavities have been reported in other early-type galaxies. Any genuine sub-beam depression would be diluted by surrounding disk material within the same resolution element, biasing the observed profile toward flatness regardless of the true underlying structure; the apertures tested here can only probe structure at the beam scale and larger, not the cavity scale itself. Second, the HCN(1-0) cube is a "representative bandwidth" product with reduced velocity coverage, and the flux extraction here was necessarily built around a fixed velocity window matched to the searched channel range. If dense gas near the nucleus is present but spread across a wider line width, offset in velocity, or otherwise diluted by this restricted spectral coverage, the resulting non-detection would reflect a bandwidth limitation rather than an absence of gas. These two limitations compound: a spatially diluted and spectrally under-sampled signal is doubly disadvantaged relative to a compact, narrow line, making the current upper limits difficult to interpret as constraining the true dense-gas surface density near the nucleus.

Resolving this ambiguity would require HCN(1-0) (or a comparably dense-gas tracer) observations that improve on both limiting factors simultaneously. A higher-resolution follow-up, with a synthesized beam of order 0.3-0.5 arcsec (roughly 25-40 pc at the adopted 16.5 Mpc distance), would bring the angular resolution close enough to the putative cavity scale to directly test for a central depression rather than a beam-diluted average. Independently, a full science-bandwidth observation with wider velocity coverage than the representative-bandwidth cube used here, and ideally somewhat deeper integration, would guard against missing dense gas that is broad-lined, kinematically offset, or simply fainter than the current sensitivity permits. Combining these two improvements — finer resolution and fuller spectral coverage in a single deeper observation — would allow a future analysis to determine whether the nucleus of NGC 4429 hosts a true dense-gas cavity coexisting with its compact continuum source, or whether the apparent HCN(1-0) faintness reported here is instead an artifact of the modest depth and coarse beam of the currently available archival products.
